name: Workplace situational judgement scenarios
status: Draft scoring key written for the prototype. It must be reviewed by at least three expert raters (target Cohen's kappa >= 0.60) before use in data collection.
instruction: Choose what you would most likely do, not what you think is the best answer.
weight_meaning: +1 = the option signals a higher level of the trait, -1 = a lower level, missing = no signal

scenarios.text: Two teammates are arguing about which framework to use for your group project, and the meeting is going nowhere.

options.text: Ask each of them to list the pros and cons, then let the whole team vote.
Make the decision yourself based on what you think is technically best, to keep things moving.
Stay out of it and wait for them to settle it between themselves.
Suggest trying a newer framework that none of you has used yet, which might suit the project better.

scenarios.text: Two days before a deadline you realise one important feature of your project will not be finished in time.

options.text: Work late both nights so that everything is finished exactly as planned.
Tell your lecturer or team lead now and agree on a smaller scope you can deliver well.
Keep going as normal and hope it comes together, even though you feel worried about it.
Build a quick creative workaround that shows the idea, even if it is not polished.

scenarios.text: Your supervisor criticises your report in front of the rest of the team.

options.text: Thank them, ask for specific examples, and revise the report.
Explain straight away why you made the choices you did.
Say very little, but keep thinking about the comments for days afterwards.
Take it as a reason to try a completely different structure for the report.

scenarios.text: A client asks you to build a small app, but their requirements are vague and incomplete.

options.text: Write a list of questions and arrange a meeting to clarify everything before you start.
Build a quick prototype of your own interpretation and show it to them for feedback.
Start coding from your best guess and adjust later if needed.
Feel uneasy and put off starting until someone gives you clearer instructions.

scenarios.text: A new member of your team keeps falling behind on their tasks and seems stressed.

options.text: Offer to sit with them and help them catch up.
Let the team leader know about the delay so the plan can be adjusted.
Quietly redo their part yourself so that the work gets done properly.
Leave it to them; managing their own work is their responsibility.

scenarios.text: The day before an important demo, the project database crashes and the data is lost.

options.text: Stay calm, follow the steps to restore a backup, and check everything carefully.
Call the team together straight away to solve it as a group.
Feel panicked and find it hard to concentrate, but keep trying to fix it.
Try an unusual fix you read about once but have never tested.

scenarios.text: Your department is holding an industry networking evening with professionals from several companies.

options.text: Go and introduce yourself to as many professionals as you can.
Go, with specific questions prepared for two or three companies you have researched.
Skip it; you would rather research the companies online on your own.
Go mainly to hear about new technologies and ideas, whoever is presenting.

scenarios.text: Your project needs a technology that nobody in the team has used before.

options.text: Volunteer to learn it and explore what else it can do.
Make a study plan with milestones and follow it step by step.
Suggest using a tool the team already knows, even if it fits the project less well.
Worry that you will not learn it fast enough and ask someone else to take it on.

scenarios.text: Your group is praised for a project, but one member did much less work than everyone else.

options.text: Accept the praise as a team; it is not worth causing tension.
Privately tell that member you noticed, and agree how work will be shared next time.
Let the lecturer know who did which part of the work.
Feel annoyed about it for a while, but say nothing.

scenarios.text: You have a free week between semesters with no assignments.

options.text: Start a creative side project just to try something new.
Plan the week to get ahead on next semester's modules.
Spend most of it meeting friends and going out.
Volunteer to help with a community project or a classmate's work.
